title: Finite subsets of a schematic homogeneous space have affine neighbourhoods
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $G$ be a separated finite-type $k$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-proper-morphism, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and let $Y$ be a separated finite-type $k$-scheme [def-pc-scheme]. Suppose a $k$-morphism $a:G\times_kY\to Y$ defines a left action: $a(1,y)=y$ and $a(g,a(h,y))=a(gh,y)$ on every test scheme. Suppose $o\in Y(k)$ [def-pc-rational-point] and that its orbit morphism $q:G\to Y$, $g\mapsto a(g,o)$, is flat, surjective and locally of finite presentation [def-weil-flat-morphism, def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation]. Then every finite subset of the underlying point set of $Y$ is contained in an affine open subscheme of $Y$. This asserts a property of the given scheme $Y$; it does not assert existence of a quotient scheme.

source.place: Appendix B, Theorem B.37, Step 2, printed p.605; closed-point formulation extended to finite point sets by closed specialization in a finite-type scheme over a field. The orbit map is an fppf quotient by the stabilizer of o. Step 2 uses only the existing homogeneous scheme, not the quasi-projectivity assumption needed earlier in Step 1.

proof.text: Let $E\subseteq |Y|$ be finite. If $E=\varnothing$, the empty open $\operatorname{Spec}(0)$ suffices. Otherwise, for each $x\in E$, the Jacobson statement applied to the nonempty closed subset $\overline{\{x\}}$ supplies a point $c_x$ closed in $Y$. Put $S=\{c_x:x\in E\}$. An open containing $c_x$ contains $x$, since opens are stable under generalization. It is therefore enough to find an affine open containing $S$. The finite-type scheme $Y$ is Noetherian (a field is a Noetherian ring). It has finitely many irreducible components; it is quasi-separated because it is separated and finite type over the affine scheme $\operatorname{Spec}k$. Apply the generic-point affine-neighbourhood lemma to all its component generic points, with the given point $o$. We obtain an affine open $U$ containing those generic points. Thus $U$ is dense in $Y$.

Apply the simultaneous rational-lift lemma to the surjective $k$-morphism $q:G\to Y$ and $S$. Choose a finite extension $K/k$ and $g_1,\ldots,g_r\in G_K(K)$ such that the points $x_j=q_K(g_j)$ are exactly the points of $S_K=p_Y^{-1}(S)$, all $K$-rational. Here $p_Y:Y_K\to Y$ is the projection. Repetitions do not affect the construction. Finite type of $G$ and $Y$, surjectivity of $q$, and closedness and finiteness of $S$ are exactly the hypotheses of that lemma.

For each finite extension $F/k$, the scalar projection $Y_F\to Y$ is locally the finite-free ring map $A\to A\otimes_k F$, hence is finite and flat. The field map $k\to F$ is finitely presented: choose a finite basis starting with $1$, use a variable for each remaining basis vector, and impose its finitely many multiplication-table relations; these relations reduce every monomial to the basis and give precisely $F$. Thus $\operatorname{Spec}F\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is flat and locally finitely presented. It is surjective since both spectra have one point; its scheme base changes are surjective by the base-change lemma and open by the flat-lfp openness lemma. In particular $U_K=p_Y^{-1}(U)$ is dense: the image of a nonempty open of $Y_K$ is a nonempty open of $Y$, so meets $U$. The base-changed $q_K$ is likewise surjective and open (the latter follows from the original flat-lfp hypotheses). Therefore $V=q_K^{-1}(U_K)$ is a dense open of $G_K$: every nonempty open has nonempty open image meeting $U_K$.

For $h\in G_K(K)$, left multiplication $t_h$ and inversion $i$ on $G_K$ are isomorphisms, with inverses $t_{h^{-1}}$ and $i$. Hence each $g_j i(V)$ is dense open. The finite intersection $\Omega=\bigcap_{j=1}^r g_j i(V)$ is dense open and nonempty because $G_K$ contains its identity. Finite intersections of dense opens are dense: successively intersect a given nonempty open with each one. The scheme $G_K$ is of finite type over $K$ by finite-type base-change stability; its closed points are dense by the Jacobson statement. Choose a closed point $b\in\Omega$. The closed-point residue-field lemma gives a finite extension $L=\kappa(b)$ of $K$, and the canonical $L$-point of $G_K$ at $b$ gives $g\in G(L)$ lying in $\Omega_L$. The extension $L/k$ is finite as a composite of finite-dimensional extensions. This choice works over finite or imperfect fields.

All the points above $S$ in $Y_L$ are the base changes of the $K$-rational $x_j$: the scheme fibre over a $K$-rational point is $\operatorname{Spec}K$, whose extension to $L$ is $\operatorname{Spec}L$. For each $j$, membership $g\in g_{j,L}i(V_L)$ says $g=g_{j,L}v_j^{-1}$ for an $L$-point $v_j\in V_L$, equivalently $g_{j,L}=gv_j$. This is valid on $L$-points because inversion and translation are scheme isomorphisms. The action identity gives $q_L(g_{j,L})=a_L(g,q_L(v_j))\in gU_L$. On $Y_L$, the map $y\mapsto a_L(g,y)$ is an isomorphism with inverse $y\mapsto a_L(g^{-1},y)$ by the action axioms. The open $A=gU_L$ is consequently affine and contains the entire finite set $S_L=p^{-1}(S)$, where $p:Y_L\to Y$. Affineness of $U_L$ follows from the affine scalar-extension formula applied to $U=\operatorname{Spec}B$: $U_L=\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_k L)$.

Use the canonical descent datum of $Y_L=Y\times_k\operatorname{Spec}L$ along $p_0:\operatorname{Spec}L\to\operatorname{Spec}k$. On test schemes, transport changes the $L$-structure and retains the map to $Y$; the identity and cocycle laws are identities of these projections. In the norm-shrinking lemma take its base $X=\operatorname{Spec}L$, $Y=\operatorname{Spec}k$, and its $V=Y_L$. Its cartesian relation object $R=Y_L\times_k\operatorname{Spec}L$ identifies with $Y_L\times_Y Y_L$; source and target become the two projections $s,t:R\to Y_L$. Since $p_0$ is finite, flat and locally of finite presentation by Step 3, its hypotheses hold. The set $S_L$ is finite, is contained in $A$, and is saturated: $s^{-1}(p^{-1}S)=t^{-1}(p^{-1}S)$ since $ps=pt$. The cited lemma supplies an affine open $W\subseteq A$ containing $S_L$ with $s^{-1}W=t^{-1}W$.

The map $p:Y_L\to Y$ is finite, flat, surjective and quasi-compact by Step 3 (on an affine chart its inverse image is one affine). Apply invariant-open image descent to $W\hookrightarrow Y_L$ and $p$. It gives an open $B=p(W)\subseteq Y$, with $p^{-1}B=W$ and $W\simeq B\times_k\operatorname{Spec}L$ as schemes. Since $p$ is surjective and $W$ contains $p^{-1}S$, one has $S\subseteq B$. The singleton $\{\operatorname{Spec}L\to\operatorname{Spec}k\}$ is an fpqc covering: it is flat, and its sole affine source covers the sole point of its affine target. Apply fpqc descent of affine morphisms to $B\to\operatorname{Spec}k$; its pullback is the affine scheme $W$. Hence $B$ is affine, contains $S$, and therefore contains $E$ by Step 1. No quotient-existence theorem, smoothness, or quasi-projectivity has been used.

Source: I read Milne iAG2017 B.37 Step 2 (printed p.605) together with Steps 1 and 3 and Remark B.38. The given flat, surjective, lfp orbit map q is used exactly as Milne uses u; quasi-projectivity is needed only in Step 1, for the existence of the quotient. Step checks: (1) Jacobson closed specializations reduce to closed points; Y is Noetherian, has finitely many components and is quasi-separated; the generic-point affine-neighbourhood lemma gives a dense affine U. (2) The new node applies to q and S, and its all-points-over-S clause is what Step 5 needs. (3) The finite-free scalar-extension clause plus flat-lfp openness and surjectivity after base change show that U_K and V=q_K^{-1}U_K are dense. (4) Ω is a finite intersection of translated dense opens, nonempty because G_K contains the identity; the Jacobson property gives a closed point b, and closed-point-field clause (a) only gives L=κ(b) finite over K and g∈Ω_L(L). (5) g_{j,L}=g v_j, so q_L(g_{j,L})=a(g,q_L(v_j))∈gU_L; the fibre over a K-rational point is Spec L, so S_L⊆A=gU_L, which is affine. (6) Norm-shrinking with p=Spec L→Spec k, V=Y_L, R≅Y_L×_Y Y_L; S_L=p^{-1}S is saturated, giving an invariant affine W. (7) Invariant-open image gives B=p(W) with W≅B_L; fpqc descent of affineness along {Spec L→Spec k} shows B is affine and contains S and E. New node lem-sfb-finite-closed-set-rational-lifts is true: lift to closed z_s and take a finite normal K containing each κ(z_s); every residue field of κ⊗K is then K, and surjectivity on fibres gives the lifts. I tested k=ℝ with ℂ-points, a purely inseparable F_p(t) case and empty S. It is statement-only, self-contained and its definitions are cited; it is not a clause of the item; DAG scans for rational lifts and finite-set affine neighbourhoods found no duplicate (lem-pd-invariant-affine-neighbourhoods assumes V is already AF).
